slides.title: Introduction
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: When modeling relationships between variables, the nature of the data that have been collected has an important bearing on the appropriate choice of an econometric model Two features of time-series data to consider: Time-series observations on a given economic unit, observed over a number of time periods, are likely to be correlated Time-series data have a natural ordering according to time

slides.title: Introduction
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: There is also the possible existence of dynamic relationships between variables A dynamic relationship is one in which the change in a variable now has an impact on that same variable, or other variables, in one or more future time periods These effects do not occur instantaneously but are spread, or distributed, over future time periods

slides.title: Introduction
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: Ways to model the dynamic relationship: Specify that a dependent variable y is a function of current and past values of an explanatory variable x y t = f left(x t, x t-1 , x t-2 , ldots right) Because of the existence of these lagged effects, this equation is called a distributed lag (DL) model

slides.title: Introduction
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: Ways to model the dynamic relationship (Continued): Capturing the dynamic characteristics of time-series by specifying a model with a lagged dependent variable as one of the explanatory variables y t = f left(y t-1 , x t right) or y t = f left(y t-1 , x t, x t-1 , x t-2 right) Such models are called autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) models, with ‘‘autoregressive’’ meaning a regression of yt on its own lag or lags

slides.title: Introduction
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: Ways to model the dynamic relationship (Continued): Model the continuing impact of change over several periods via the error term y t = f left(x t right) + e t qquad qquad e t = f left(e t-1 right) In this case et is correlated with et - 1 We say the errors are serially correlated or autocorrelated

slides.title: Introduction
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: The primary assumption in OLS is: mathrm cov left(y i, y j right) = mathrm cov left(e i, e j right) = 0 quad text for i neq j For time series, this is written as: mathrm cov left(y t, y s right) = mathrm cov left(e t, e s right) = 0 quad text for t neq s The dynamic models mentioned previously imply correlation between yt and yt - 1 or et and et - 1 or both, so they clearly violate this assumption

slides.title: Finite Distributed Lags
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: Consider a linear model in which, after q time periods, changes in x no longer have an impact on y y t = alpha + beta 0 x t + beta 1 x t-1 + beta 2 x t-2 + cdots + beta q x t-q + e t This model has two uses: Forecasting y T+1 = alpha + beta 0 x T+1 + beta 1 x T + beta 2 x T-1 + cdots + beta q x T-q+1 + e T+1 Policy analysis frac partial E(y t) partial x t-s = frac partial E(y t+s ) partial x t = beta s What is the effect of a change in x on y?

slides.title: Finite Distributed Lags
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: The effect of a one-unit change in xt is distributed over the current and next q periods, from which we get the term ‘‘distributed lag model’’ y t = alpha + beta 0 x t + beta 1 x t-1 + beta 2 x t-2 + cdots + beta q x t-q + e t It is called a finite distributed lag model of order q It is assumed that after a finite number of periods q, changes in x no longer have an impact on y The coefficient βs is called a distributed-lag weight or an s-period delay multiplier The coefficient β0 (s = 0) is called the impact multiplier

slides.title: Finite Distributed Lags
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: Assume xt is increased by one unit and then maintained at its new level in subsequent periods y t = alpha + beta 0 x t + beta 1 x t-1 + beta 2 x t-2 + cdots + beta q x t-q + e t The immediate impact will be β0 the total effect in period t + 1 will be β0 + β1, in period t + 2 it will be β0 + β1 + β2, and so on These quantities are called interim multipliers The total multiplier is the final effect on y of the sustained increase after q or more periods have elapsed sum s=0 q beta s

slides.title: Estimation with Serially Correlated Errors
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: Least squares estimation without recognizing the existence of serially correlated errors The least squares estimator is still a linear unbiased estimator, but it is no longer best The formulas for the standard errors usually computed for the least squares estimator are no longer correct Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests that use these standard errors may be misleading

slides.title: Autoregressive Distributed Lag Models
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: An autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) model is one that contains both lagged xt’s and lagged yt’s y t = delta + delta 0 x t + delta 1 x t-1 + cdots + delta q x t-q + theta 1 y t-1 + cdots + theta p y t-p + v t begin aligned mathrm ARDL left(1,1 right): widehat INF t = 0.3336 + 0.5593 ,INF t-1 - 0.6882 ,DU t + 0.3200 ,DU t-1 mathrm ARDL left(1,0 right): widehat INF t = 0.3548 + 0.5282 ,INF t-1 - 0.4909 ,DU t end aligned Two examples: An ARDL (p,q) model can be transformed into one with only lagged x’s which go back into the infinite past: y t = alpha + beta 0 x t + beta 1 x t-1 + beta 2 x t-2 + beta 3 x t-3 + cdots + e t = alpha + sum s=0 infty beta s x t-s + e t This model is called an infinite distributed lag model

slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: stationary variables
slides.text: Four possible criteria for choosing p and q: Has serial correlation in the errors been eliminated? Are the signs and magnitudes of the estimates consistent with our expectations from theory? Are the estimates significantly different from zero, particularly those at the longest lags? What values for p and q minimize information criteria such as the AIC and SC?

slides.title: Unit Root Tests for Stationarity
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: non-stationary variables
slides.text: The AR(1) process yt = ρyt-1 + vt is stationary when |ρ| < 1 We want to test whether ρ is equal to one (nonstationary) or significantly less than one (stationary) Tests for this purpose are known as unit root tests for stationarity Dickey–Fuller test is the most commonly used one

slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: non-stationary variables

slides.title: Unit Root Tests for Stationarity
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: non-stationary variables
slides.text: The Dickey-Fuller testing procedure: First plot the time series of the variable and select a suitable Dickey-Fuller test based on a visual inspection of the plot If the series appears to be wandering or fluctuating around a sample average of zero, use Delta y t = gamma y t-1 + v t If the series appears to be wandering or fluctuating around a sample average which is nonzero, use Delta y t = alpha + gamma y t-1 + v t If the series appears to be wandering or fluctuating around a linear trend, use Delta y t = alpha + gamma y t-1 + lambda t + v t Second, proceed with one of the unit root tests

slides.title: Cointegration
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: non-stationary variables
slides.text: Definition: If et = yt - β1 - β2xt is a stationary I(0) process, yt and xt are said to be cointegrated Cointegration implies that yt and xt share similar stochastic trends, and, since the difference et is stationary, they never diverge too far from each other In this case regression analysis is valid. No concerns about spurious regression. The test for stationarity of the residuals is based on the test equation: Delta hat e t = gamma hat e t-1 + v t Critical values vary according to regression model

slides.title: Regression When There Is No Cointegration
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: non-stationary variables
slides.text: We need to convert nonstationary, non-cointegrated series to stationary series The technique depends on whether the variables are difference stationary ( ) or y t = alpha + y t-1 + v t y t = alpha + delta t + v t trend stationary ( ) Delta y t = alpha + v t Difference stationary: first differencing Trend stationary: de-trending y t - alpha - delta t = v t

slides.title: Summary
slides.topicname: Regression with time series data: non-stationary variables
slides.text: If variables are stationary, or I(1) and cointegrated, we can estimate a regression relationship between the levels of those variables without fear of encountering a spurious regression If the variables are I(1) and not cointegrated, we need to estimate a relationship in first differences, with or without the constant term If they are trend stationary, we can either de-trend the series first and then perform regression analysis with the stationary (de-trended) variables or, alternatively, estimate a regression relationship that includes a trend variable

slides.title: The ARCH Model
slides.topicname: Time-varying volatility and ARCH models
slides.text: Autoregressive conditional heteroskedastic (ARCH) model Deals with stationary series, but with conditional variances that change over time Consider a model with an AR(1) error term: v t sim N(0, sigma v 2) e t = rho e t-1 + v t, qquad | rho| < 1 y t = phi + e t, The unconditional mean of the error is: E left[e t right] = E left[v t + rho v t-1 + rho 2 v t-2 + cdots right] = 0 The conditional mean for the error is: E left[e t mid I t-1 right] = E left[ rho e t-1 mid I t-1 right] + E left[v t right] = rho e t-1

slides.title: The ARCH Model
slides.topicname: Time-varying volatility and ARCH models
slides.text: The unconditional variance of the error is: begin aligned E left[e t - 0 right] 2 = E left[v t + rho v t-1 + rho 2 v t-2 + cdots right] 2 = E left[v t 2 + rho 2 v t-1 2 + rho 4 v t-2 2 + cdots right] = sigma v 2 left[1 + rho 2 + rho 4 + cdots right] = frac sigma v 2 1- rho 2 end aligned The conditional variance for the error is: E left[ left(e t - rho e t-1 right) 2 mid I t-1 right] = E left[v t 2 mid I t-1 right] = sigma v 2

slides.title: The ARCH Model
slides.topicname: Time-varying volatility and ARCH models
slides.text: Suppose that instead of a conditional mean that changes over time we have a conditional variance that changes over time y t = phi + e t, e t mid I t-1 sim N(0, h t) Consider the AR(1) model on slide 7: h t = alpha 0 + alpha 1 e t-1 2, qquad alpha 0 > 0, quad 0 le alpha 1 < 1 ARCH: time-varying variances (heteroskedasticity) that depend on (are conditional on) lagged effects (autocorrelation)

slides.title: The ARCH Model
slides.topicname: Time-varying volatility and ARCH models
slides.text: The AR(1) model is now an ARCH (1) model y t = phi + e t, e t mid I t-1 sim N(0, h t) h t = alpha 0 + alpha 1 e t-1 2, qquad alpha 0 > 0, quad 0 le alpha 1 < 1 The standardized errors are standard normal: left( frac e t sqrt h t , middle| , I t-1 right) = z sim N(0,1) ~ N(0,1) We can write: begin aligned E left(e t right) = E left(z t right) E left( sqrt alpha 0 + alpha 1 e t-1 2 right) = 0 E left(e t 2 right) = E left(z t 2 right) E left( alpha 0 + alpha 1 e t-1 2 right) = alpha 0 + alpha 1 E left(e t-1 2 right) end aligned

slides.title: The ARCH Model
slides.topicname: Time-varying volatility and ARCH models
slides.text: The ARCH model is useful for modeling volatility and especially changes in volatility over time The ARCH model is intuitively appealing because it seems sensible to explain volatility as a function of the errors et These errors are often called ‘‘shocks’’ or ‘‘news’’ by financial analysts They represent the unexpected According to the ARCH model, the larger the shock, the greater the volatility in the series This model captures volatility clustering, as big changes in et are fed into further big changes in ht via the lagged effect et-1

slides.title: Extensions
slides.topicname: Time-varying volatility and ARCH models
slides.text: From ARCH(1) to ARCH(q): Functional form: h t = alpha 0 + alpha 1 e t-1 2 + alpha 2 e t-2 2 ldots + alpha q e t-q 2 Testing, estimating, and forecasting, are natural extensions of the case with one lag One of the shortcomings of an ARCH(q) model is that there are q + 1 parameters to estimate, which may lose accuracy in the estimation The generalized ARCH model, or GARCH, is an alternative way to capture long lagged effects with fewer parameters

slides.title: Extensions
slides.topicname: Time-varying volatility and ARCH models
slides.text: From ARCH(q) to GARCH (1, 1) model h t = alpha 0 + alpha 1 e t-1 2 + alpha 2 e t-2 2 ldots + alpha q e t-q 2 begin aligned h t = alpha 0 + alpha 1 e t-1 2 + beta 1 alpha 1 e t-2 2 + beta 1 2 alpha 1 e t-3 2 + cdots [2pt] text or [2pt] h t = left( alpha 0 - beta 1 alpha 0 right) + alpha 1 e t-1 2 + beta 1 left( alpha 0 + alpha 1 e t-2 2 + beta 1 alpha 1 e t-3 2 + cdots right) [2pt] text but, since: [2pt] h t-1 = alpha 0 + alpha 1 e t-2 2 + beta 1 alpha 1 e t-3 2 + beta 1 2 alpha 1 e t-4 2 + cdots [2pt] text we get: quad h t = delta + alpha 1 e t-1 2 + beta 1 h t-1 end aligned Re-write as: h t = delta + alpha 1 e t-1 2 + beta 1 h t-1

slides.topicname: Time-varying volatility and ARCH models
slides.text: GARCH (1, 1) model The model is a very popular specification because it fits many data series well It tells us that the volatility changes with lagged shocks (e2 t-1) but there is also momentum in the system working via ht-1 One reason why this model is so popular is that it can capture long lags in the shocks with only a few parameters
